region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San ethnographic summary; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1921

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel III (1921), No. 56

summary.en: Von Wielligh's summary of Bushman belief: the old race ('Chwe-'na-ssho-'ke) could change into any animal, tree or person; the sun is a murdered man's head thrown into the sky; the moon is the Mantis's shoe that dies and revives; the hollow moon carries the newly dead, who come alive with it; death became permanent only through the Hare's quarrel; the Morning Star is Dawn's heart and the Evening Star Evening-gleam's heart; and a great star once sang all the stars their names.
summary.zh: 范威利赫之桑人信仰撮要：古族（'楚那索克）可化為任何獸、樹、人；日乃被弒者之首擲天而成；月乃螳螂之鞋，死而復生；空月承載新死者，隨月復活；死亡之恆久僅因野兔之爭；晨星為曙光之心、昏星為暮光之心；一大星曾唱出眾星之名。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic summary written by G. R. von Wielligh from his own Bushman informants; presented as an archival record of colonial-era fieldwork.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel III No. 56 (1921); not verbatim. Of a Supreme Being, of a place of Happiness or of Punishment the Bushman has no conception at all. His outgoing thought seems to be that in the beginning there existed an old race of Bushmen; to it all owe their existence. He knows the old race as 'Chwe-'na-ssho-'ke, who could change themselves into any animal, tree or person. In the beginning there was a twilight over the whole earth; the sun, moon and stars arose only later.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 56; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The sun is one of the old race, with a shining face, whom the others murdered; the children, at their mothers' command, threw the head of the sun-man into the sky, where it still is. Morning after morning the head rises on the east and seeks its body, which has become a crab, till evening, and sleeps in the west to wake again the next morning. The moon is the shoe of the 'Hotnotsgod which the whirlwind blew into the sky; the hollow of the horned moon is the receiving place of the newly dead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 56; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. As the moon grows again to full moon the corpses come alive again by the power of the moonwater; and as the moon becomes full and has no more place for the revived persons, those persons descend to the earth and come alive again whenever they die — just as the moon comes alive month after month. Thus death was at first only a temporary sleep. But death — so as not to come alive again — came into the world through the Hare, who strove with the Moon and was split-lipped; hence the superstition of the piece of sinew-flesh in the hare's thigh that has remained human flesh, which Bushmen do not eat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 56; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Morning Star is the heart of Daybreak and the Evening Star the heart of Evening-gleam; the other great stars are living beings, and the little stars also live. One great star gave, in a song, all the stars their names... When a notable person dies, a great heap of stones is piled over his grave, and that stone-heap is honoured for the sake of the spirit that dwells in it; when one buries someone a 'laying-down prayer' is first spoken before the funeral procession leaves the grave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 56; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San ethnographic summary; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1921

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel III (1921), No. 57

summary.en: Animal superstitions: the Water-Snake dries up springs before white hunters; a serpent-stone draws poison from a bite; the jackal's heart makes children cowards; ostrich lungs must be eaten raw by children for a big voice; a beheaded snake crawls home to hide in its killer's bedding; springbok possess invisible arrows; meat of slow game makes hunters' aim true; and snakes near graves bring good tidings.
summary.zh: 動物迷信：水蛇於白人獵者前涸泉；蛇石可吸毒；豺心使童懦怯；童須生食鴕肺以得巨聲；斷首之蛇爬回藏於仇者床褥；跳羚具無形之箭；食緩獸之肉使射者命中；墓旁之蛇報吉訊。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic summary by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel III No. 57 (1921); not verbatim. The Great Water-Snake has a glittering stone on its head and the power to make fountains fill or dry up. He listens well to the Bushman sorcerers and follows the hunters under the ground everywhere in the waterless regions; where he is the fountains overflow, or he brings the water up to just under the surface so the hunters need only dig a shallow hole... As soon as white hunters follow the game into the desert, the Bushmen have only to speak with the Great Water-Snake, and he lets the strongest fountain dry up before the eyes of the whites.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 57; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The heart of the jackal is never given to children to eat, for a jackal is very timid; if children eat the heart they become cowards... If a Bushman shoots an ostrich, his children must eat the lungs of the ostrich raw; for if the lungs are cooked they lose the property of giving the children a big voice — the Bushmen find the booming of an ostrich finer than the roaring of a lion.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 57; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. If someone wounds a snake, or even only breaks its head from the body a little way, that snake comes to the house of the person who hurt it, hides itself somewhere in a corner, in his bedding or in his veld-shoe, and lies there ready to bite the person dead. The Bushmen do not let their children play on fresh springbok skins, nor let fresh blood or flesh touch bow, arrow or quiver; for then the spirit of the springbok draws into the children or the owner of the bow and arrow, and the springboks in the veld become wild toward such people... The springbok possesses invisible arrows with which it can shoot a person unnoticed; they go inside the body and make him sick, and when he is sick he always shoots wide.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 57; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When a snake is seen by a grave it must be respected and not killed, for it brings good tidings of the one buried there, or brings good tidings to the spirit of the dead person... To make rain only the maids strike with stones on the ground; the Rain-Beast hears the stamping and then lets rain come through a thunderstorm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 57; not verbatim.

title.en: More Superstitions: Weather, Dreams and Ghosts

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San ethnographic summary; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1921

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel III (1921), No. 58

summary.en: The lightning kills with stones; look straight at the flash and its eye respects yours. The Wind-bird avenges stone-throwing with a storm; toadstools are the rain's children and must be set down gently; music in a storm draws the thunderbolt; a fist-sized stone heated in the ashes burns bad dreams; and a shooting star with a long train tells of a far friend's death.
summary.zh: 雷以石殺人；直視閃光者，其電乃避其目。風鳥遭擲石則起暴風報復；傘菌乃雨之子，須輕放；雷時奏樂者引雷石；拳大之石入火灰可焚惡夢；長尾流星預告遠方友人之死。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic summary by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel III No. 58 (1921); not verbatim. The Bushman has great awe of thunder, wind and storms... He believes the thunder can kill a person with stones. If the flash is sharp, one must look at the lightning, and one's eyes shine like the lightning itself, and then the ray of light will have respect for the eyes of the person who looks at it and will not strike him dead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 58; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The wind is made by a bird, the Wind-bird, with its wings and blowing. If anyone throws stones, kieries or sand at the Wind-bird, or shoots arrows at him, he makes that bird angry, and the maker of the wind lets a storm arise to destroy and tear everything apart... Toadstools and other mushroom growths are the children of the rain; if anyone pulls them out he must not throw them about but set them down gently, otherwise the rain grows angry and calls up a storm that washes everything away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 58; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. To get rid of the evil consequences of dreams the Bushmen seek a stone as big as their fist, hold it in the hand, talk to it and tell the bad dreams they had in the night; then they blow their breath on the stone and quickly push it under the warm ashes and coals, so that the dreams must burn. If they do not do this, the bad dreams go with them into the field and tell everything to the game, the Bushman-rice and the veld-food, so that the dreamer finds it all bad in the field and comes home disappointed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 58; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Bushman is very much afraid of ghosts; near a burial place one does not get him in the dark. If he thinks he sees a ghost, he pulls out a bush, sets it upside down with the roots up, and runs away as hard as he can; for if the ghost sees a bush standing upside down, he imagines the bush grew so, stands there marvelling how it can grow — and when a wind blows the bush over, the ghost springs away and returns to the one who planted it, seeing it is all humbug. And if a star shoots — especially with a long train of light — the Bushmen believe a friend or acquaintance has died; the star shows where the person lives, and a few days later the sad tidings come.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel III (1921), No. 58; not verbatim.

title.en: Krappies and the Ghost in the Churchyard

region.zh: 開普殖民地農莊（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition; told to G. R. von Wielligh by Oom Karel and Piet M., published 1922

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel IV (1922), No. 95

summary.en: Krappies, a superstitious Bushman servant, tends his master's grave flowers faithfully; on New Year's Eve he drinks by mistake a bottle of spirits, wakes in the churchyard, sees an owl on the grave and his dead master standing with a bottle — 'Krappies, Krappies, what is this?' — and a goat at the gate. The ghost haunts his room; he falls sick, confesses, and never touches drink again, believing the master's spirit came to set him right.
summary.zh: 迷信之桑僕克拉皮忠心照料主墓之花；除夕誤飲烈酒，醒於墓園，見墓上之鴞與手持酒瓶之亡主——「克拉皮，克拉皮，此為何物？」——門前又有山羊。亡靈夜擾其室；他病倒、吐實、滴酒不沾，深信主人之靈來懲其過。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; colonial setting; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel IV No. 95 (1922); not verbatim. Krappies was a particularly sly little fellow and soon became the favourite of the master's children; he was very superstitious, and that was too fine for the children, so they could play many more jokes with him. He was dead-honest in his way, but not with tobacco and strong drink — there he stole wherever a chance offered.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 95; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Oom Willem's wife died and was buried in the family churchyard on the farm; the master called Krappies and told him the old missus had always been so good to him, and now he must see that the white flower-trees always got water... Krappies tended the churchyard and let no blade of grass grow; and when Oom Willem died soon after and was buried beside his wife, Krappies clung all the more to the churchyard, for he believed the spirits of his master and missus blessed him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 95; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. On New Year's Eve Krappies worked the whole day alone in the churchyard and got a dop of wine at noon; but under the cypress tree lay, by mistake, spirits of wine instead of brandy. 'Aha, that is the real stuff for you!' He drank, dozed off, and woke in the dark completely confused — in the churchyard. On the old missus's gravestone sat an owl; under the cypress tree stood the old master with the bottle in his hand, asking: 'Krappies, Krappies, what is this?'; and at the little gate a goat blocked his way. He burst through and ran to his room, and the old master's ghost stayed that night in his room. The next day he lay sick, and at last told the whole story; Oom Karel and Oom Piet made it clear to him that it was the spirit of the old master who had come to set him right. He believed it so firmly that he never again put his mouth to strong drink.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 95; not verbatim.

title.en: Bles and the Sorcerers of the Red-Stone Mine
title.zh: 布列斯與紅石礦之巫者

region.zh: 南非北開普省後哈坦姆（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition; told to G. R. von Wielligh by Ou Bles in 1882, published 1922

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel IV (1922), No. 96

summary.en: The old race buried red ochre in a hole in the mountain-side where fierce sorcerers dwell; hunters chew kou-wood that lets them see the old sorcerers unseen, stone the holes as they dig, and club the air as they walk away. A spy-bird turns out to be a sorcerer starling, a great male baboon and his two mates the sorcerers themselves, shot dead by all three bows.
summary.zh: 古族藏紅赭石於山腹之穴，中有兇巫居住；獵者嚼口烏木，得見古巫而巫不見彼；掘時擲石鎮穴，歸途沿途擊空。偵察之鳥竟為巫者化之椋鳥；大雄狒狒與二伴即巫者化身，三弓齊射殺之。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel IV No. 96 (1922); not verbatim. Far up the slope of a mountain is a digging-place for red ochre. The Bushmen of our time always went there to fetch red ochre with which to make their bodies red, colour their knitted skins, and paint people and animals on the rocks. The man who had red ochre was a rich man, for he traded with it among far-dwelling Bushmen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 96; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. They say that in that mountain many fierce sorcerers live, and that they sometimes had to fight hard with those sorcerers over the red ochre. In the days of long ago the old race dug a hole on the slope of the mountain, made red ochre, and stored it in that hole; they hid many other things in holes too, for they lived in that mountain and could see well that others did not spoil their things.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 96; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Our race, with understanding, can outwit the old sorcerers: before going to the ochre diggings one goes to one of our sorcerers and asks for kou-wood-chips to chew, so that we can see the old sorcerers, but they cannot see us. As they climbed they threw stones all around to frighten the sorcerers, who see the stones fall but not whence they come; the sorcerers flee into holes — a mouse-hole, a scorpion-hole, an ant-hole, the smallest hole they can crawl into. A white-tailed starling flew out of a hole and screeched; the husband shot it with the kou-chip in his mouth; it became a great male baboon with two mates, and all three bows brought them down.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 96; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Leopard Made a Master of Them

region.zh: 南非北開普省羅格山（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition; told to G. R. von Wielligh by Ou Bles, published 1922

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel IV (1922), No. 98

summary.en: The Bushmen trap a leopard in a poisoned-stake pit and haul him out on his tail; the leaped-up leopard scalps one man with his claws, kills another, and eats the dead — while two boys sit weaponless in trees all day. At evening the best shots lure him from tree to tree and kill him: 'so the leopard kept them all day for master.'
summary.zh: 桑人於毒樁坑困豹，曳其尾而出；躍起之豹以爪剝一人之顱、殺另一人、且食其屍——二童持弓無計，終日困於樹上。傍晚善射者誘其逐樹而斃之：「豹遂以其人為主終日。」

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel IV No. 98 (1922); not verbatim. In those days there were many leopards in the Roggeveld and Bokveld mountains. The Bushmen knew how to snare them or catch them in trap-pits: under the pit they set long sharp wooden stakes, with points as hard and sharp as an awl, smeared with the same poison as their arrows; and over the pit they arranged the ground and grass with blood and placed the piece of bone-meat behind.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 98; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One morning they found the leopard stuck fast in one of the sharp stakes, dead as a stone... They took off their karosses and laid their bows and arrow-bags on the ground, took the leopard by the tail and hind legs and dragged him out. That was too much for the male who lay there near by: he sprang up, scalped one of them with his sharp claws so that the skin of his head came off almost whole, bit another dead; and the other two fled each into a tree and sat there safe but defenceless the whole day, while the leopard ate the corpse.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 98; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In the afternoon their people came to seek them; the two best shots crept near while the leopard kept looking at the place whence he had heard the voices; the two sprang each into a tree near the others, and they teased the leopard out from tree to tree till he came to where he got his death-shot. So the leopard kept them all day for master.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 98; not verbatim.

title.en: The Flute-Reed and the Singing Lion Cubs

region.zh: 南非北開普省羅格費爾德（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition; told to G. R. von Wielligh by Ou Bles, published 1922; the second tale told by J. M. Orpen (Cape Monthly Magazine, July 1874)

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel IV (1922), No. 99

summary.en: An old sorcerer guards the good flute-reed; a son who takes his own arrows instead of the burning one is bitten dead, and the lion's cubs leap over the corpse singing 'He steals our flute-reed... his father knows nothing!' The father comes with the fire-arrow; the whole burning family flees. In Orpen's Maluti version 'Kaggen's son Cogaz is hung on a tree by the baboons, who sing 'Cagn thinks he is clever'; 'Kaggen, roused by his dolosse, punctures every dancer's back with sharp skewers and drives them to the mountains as baboons — then revives his son.
summary.zh: 老巫守良笛蘆；自帶己箭而不攜火箭之子被咬斃；獅子群跳屍而歌「他偷我們的笛蘆……其父毫不知情！」父攜火箭至；焚身之獅族盡逃。奧彭之馬盧蒂版：螳螂之子科加茲遭狒狒吊於樹，唱「卡恩自以為聰明」；螳螂以算籌占得噩耗，以尖籤刺眾舞者之背，逐之為狒狒——復活其子。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh and in English by J. M. Orpen (1874); presented as an archival record. The Orpen 'Cagn' is 'Kaggen, the Mantis.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel IV No. 99 (1922); not verbatim. An old Bushman of the old race once told his son to go and fetch flute-reed to make arrows of, warning him against an old sorcerer who guarded that reed so that the old folk could not make such good arrows; and he gave the son a certain arrow with which to shoot the sorcerer, an arrow that would burn him so that he could do nothing. But the son was headstrong: he took his own arrows and left the burning arrow at home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 99; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When the son came where the good flute-reed grew he began at once to cut. The old sorcerer changed himself and his family into lions, and asked the son what he did there. 'Why did you not first ask me?' said the lion. 'I did not see you,' answered the son. Then the lion bit the son dead. The lion's three children sprang to and fro over the corpse and sang: 'He steals our flute-reed, He steals our flute-reed, To make arrows. Our father has beaten him, Our father has beaten him; His father knows nothing!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 99; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When the son stayed away too long the father said to his wife: 'Our son is dead; I can see it in my dolosse, and I must go and look.' He found the burning arrow in the hut and went to where his son lay dead. 'Now indeed I shall also bite you dead,' said the lion; but the father shot him with the fire-arrow, the bodies of the whole family caught fire, and they all fled. In Orpen's Maluti story 'Kaggen sent his eldest son Cogaz to cut sticks for bows; the baboons hung him on the top of a tree, dancing round it and singing 'Cagn thinks he is clever'; 'Kaggen, woken by his dolosse hung over his nose, went and made every dancer stoop while he drove a sharp skewer into each one's back, chased them to the mountains to live on roots, insects and scorpions as a punishment — baboons had then no tails — and took Cogaz down and revived him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 99, and J. M. Orpen, Cape Monthly Magazine (July 1874); not verbatim.

region.zh: 南非德蘭士瓦高原（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition; told to G. R. von Wielligh on the Highveld in 1883, published 1922

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel IV (1922), No. 100

summary.en: A lame Bushman herder, proud that his dung-fire chimney burns like wood, tells how a crocodile dragged him under at a hippo-hole — 'if a white man and a Bushman walk through water, the crocodile never takes the white man, but the Bushman' — how he lay dead-still in the den under the bank, got a test-bite on his leg, and squeezed himself skinny through a crack of light to freedom.
summary.zh: 跛足桑牧自豪其糞火煙囪燃如柴火，述其於河馬池遭鱷曳入水底——「白人與桑人同涉水，鱷永不取白人，唯取桑人」——他在岸下穴中僵臥如屍，被試咬其腿，最後自一線之光縫中瘦身擠出而脫。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel IV No. 100 (1922); not verbatim. 'Baas, I can see you white people and here my mate do not yet understand how to make fire with dung-balls; let me show you.' He packed the dung-balls round the fire like a chimney of eighteen inches high, and a flame leapt up in that chimney as if it were a wood fire... He pointed out the place on his leg below the knee and told his story.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 100; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. 'My work was to look after the oxen. In the stream where our standing place was there were big hippo-holes; but we did not really see crocodiles there... The blood of the game that my master's people shot, and the blood-smeared things that were continually washed in the stream, lured the crocodile. One day the little baas and I walked through the shallow water; just as we were half over, a crocodile got me by the leg under my knee and dragged me into the hippo-hole... If a white man and a Bushman walk through water, the crocodile never takes the white man, but the Bushman.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 100; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. 'The crocodile thought I was dead, for I played dead-still as he dragged me into the hole under the bank; every time he came to peep whether I still lay quiet... When my eyes had grown used to the dark and I came right, I saw a ray of light shining down through a crack; I crept softly higher and saw it was only a big crack... Just as I was ready to spring out above, the crocodile came again to peep and gave me just a sore bite on the leg — I believe to test whether I was really dead. I lay so still and breathed softly; then I took my chance and squeezed through the narrow crack, holding myself thin — and above I was out! and ran quickly away on my sore leg, clean away from his body.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel IV (1922), No. 100; not verbatim.
